adjudications.support: רשאי הוא, בהסכמת נשיא המדינה, לפזר את הכנסת בצו שיפורסם ברשומות (s. 22(a)); likewise s. 19(b): הבעת אי-אמון ... יראוה כהחלטת הכנסת על התפזרותה
adjudications.reason: Principal subject separation of powers, as both coders say. The text gives the executive a new power over the legislature's existence (s. 22: dissolution by the prime minister's order on his own finding that a majority opposes the government, subject only to the President's consent), makes the Knesset's core check self-destructive (ss. 3(d), 19(b), 20-21: rejecting the cabinet, no confidence or budget failure dissolves the Knesset, with ss. 34-35 of Basic Law: The Knesset disapplied), and lets the government spend without a budget law (s. 58, new s. 3B); each reduces the legislature's independent leverage over the executive, which is a contradiction of the value, not a rearrangement of it. It is limited rather than sharp because each shift is bounded: presidential consent, elections for both offices, the one-twelfth cap and three-month clock, and removal of the prime minister by eighty members without dissolution (s. 27). The new checks (ss. 3(c), 35(c), 39(b), 48, 49, 52, 53) and the entrenchments of elections, rule of law, core rights and court access (ss. 57, 56, 17-18, 25, 50(d)) are entrenchment, which the definition subordinates to any contradiction, so I adopt Coder B's reading.
